messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** for how you could use the two tools you described to place a “burger + fries” order at McDonald’s. I’ll walk through the logic, the kinds of API calls you’d need, and give you concrete examples of how to invoke the tools. --- ## 1. Understand the workflow | Step | What you need to do | Why it matters | |------|---------------------|----------------| | **1. Find the right API** | Search the web for a public or partner API that lets you place orders at McDonald’s (or a delivery partner that serves McDonald’s). | You can’t order without an endpoint that accepts the order payload. | | **2. Inspect the API docs** | Parse the returned documentation to learn:
• Base URL
• Authentication method
• Endpoints for menu, cart, checkout
• Required parameters (location, item IDs, quantity, payment) | Knowing the contract lets you build a valid request. | | **3. Authenticate** | If the API requires a token (OAuth, API key, session cookie), obtain it. | Most APIs won’t let you place an order without a valid auth token. | | **4. Get the menu / item IDs** | Call the “menu” endpoint to find the numeric IDs for the burger and fries you want. | The order payload usually uses IDs, not names. | | **5. Build the order payload** | Create a JSON object that lists the items, quantities, and any modifiers. | This is the core of the order. | | **6. Submit the order** | POST the payload to the “checkout” or “order” endpoint. | This actually places the order. | | **7. Handle the response** | Check for success, capture order ID, estimate delivery time, etc. | Gives you confirmation and next steps. | --- ## 2. Tool usage pattern ### 2.1 Search Tool ```text search("McDonald's ordering API burger fries") ``` - **Goal**: Pull up the official McDonald’s API docs or a partner API (e.g., DoorDash, UberEats) that supports McDonald’s. - **What to look for**: URLs, authentication flows, sample requests. ### 2.2 Execute Tool ```text execute_api_call( url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders", method="POST", headers={"Authorization":"Bearer ", "Content-Type":"application/json"}, body={ "location": {"latitude": 40.7128, "longitude": -74.0060}, "items": [ {"id":"BURGER123", "quantity":1}, {"id":"FRIES456", "quantity":1} ], "payment": {"method":"card", "token":""} } ) ``` - **Goal**: Send the actual order. - **What to watch**: HTTP status codes, error messages, required fields. --- ## 3. Concrete example (using a hypothetical DoorDash‑style API) > **NOTE**: The following is illustrative. Real APIs may differ in endpoint names, auth flow, and payload structure. ### 3.1 Search for the API ```commentary to=functions.requests_get { "url": "https://api.example.com/search", "params": {"q": "McDonald's ordering API"}, "headers": {"Accept":"application/json"} } ``` Assume the search returns a link to DoorDash’s “Restaurant Order API” docs. ### 3.2 Inspect the docs From the docs we learn: | Endpoint | Method | Description | |----------|--------|-------------| | `/v1/auth/token` | POST | Get OAuth token | | `/v1/restaurants/{id}/menu` | GET | Get menu items | | `/v1/orders` | POST | Place an order | ### 3.3 Authenticate ```commentary to=functions.requests_get { "url": "https://api.doordash.com/v1/auth/token", "method": "POST", "headers": {"Content-Type":"application/json"}, "params": { "client_id":"YOUR_CLIENT_ID", "client_secret":"YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET", "grant_type":"client_credentials" } } ``` Assume the response contains: ```json { "access_token":"abc123", "expires_in":3600 } ``` ### 3.4 Get the menu and find item IDs ```commentary to=functions.requests_get { "url": "https://api.doordash.com/v1/restaurants/12345/menu", "method": "GET", "headers": {"Authorization":"Bearer abc123"} } ``` Response snippet: ```json { "items":[ {"id":"BURGER123","name":"Big Mac","price":5.99}, {"id":"FRIES456","name":"Large Fries","price":2.49} ] } ``` ### 3.5 Build the order payload ```json { "restaurant_id":"12345", "location":{"latitude":40.7128,"longitude":-74.0060}, "items":[ {"id":"BURGER123","quantity":1}, {"id":"FRIES456","quantity":1} ], "payment":{"method":"card","token":"PAYMENT_TOKEN"} } ``` ### 3.6 Submit the order ```commentary to=functions.requests_get { "url": "https://api.doordash.com/v1/orders", "method": "POST", "headers": { "Authorization":"Bearer abc123", "Content-Type":"application/json" }, "params": { "body": { "restaurant_id":"12345", "location":{"latitude":40.7128,"longitude":-74.0060}, "items":[ {"id":"BURGER123","quantity":1}, {"id":"FRIES456","quantity":1} ], "payment":{"method":"card","token":"PAYMENT_TOKEN"} } } } ``` ### 3.7 Handle the response ```json { "order_id":"ORD7890", "status":"confirmed", "estimated_delivery":"2026-06-29T18:45:00Z", "total":8.48 } ``` If the status is `confirmed`, you’ve successfully placed the order. If you receive an error (e.g., 401 Unauthorized, 400 Bad Request), inspect the error message and adjust the request accordingly. --- ## 4. Things to keep in mind | Issue | Mitigation | |-------|------------| | **API rate limits** | Cache menu data; retry with exponential back‑off. | | **Location accuracy** | Use GPS coordinates; verify with the API’s geofencing rules. | | **Payment security** | Store payment tokens securely; never expose raw card numbers. | | **Error handling** | Parse error codes; provide user‑friendly messages. | | **Legal compliance** | Ensure you have permission to use the API; respect terms of service. | --- ## 5. Summary 1. **Search** for the ordering API (via the search tool). 2. **Parse** the returned docs to learn endpoints, auth, and payload format. 3. **Authenticate** (OAuth, API key, etc.). 4. **Retrieve** the menu to get item IDs. 5. **Build** the order JSON with your chosen items. 6. **Execute** the order POST request (via the execute tool). 7. **Confirm** the response and handle any errors. With this workflow you can programmatically place a burger and fries order at McDonald’s (or any partner restaurant) using the two tools you have.
